info.desc: Music for the Masses is the sixth studio album by Depeche Mode. Released by Mute Records on September 28, 1987, it provided the band with success in the United States for the first time since Some Great Reward, and the new styles of music that appeared on the album and its predecessor Black Celebration formed the foundation for their breakthrough effort, Violator. These three are widely considered to be the band's peak in both lyrical and musical sense, attributed to Gore's maturing songcraft and Wilder's synthesized orchestrations. podcast.body: Depeche Mode's 1987 album cover features a beige background with the band's logo and album title in stark block letters. The central image depicts three red megaphones mounted on a pole, set in an isolated location without an audience, literally "in the middle of nowhere" in England's Peak District. This concept was developed by long-time collaborator Martin Atkins, who favored megaphones and the idea of speakers in an unconventional setting, disconnected from actual "masses." The band and label embraced the concept, using megaphones throughout the album's marketing. "The image features three red megaphones, mounted on a pole, ready to broadcast to, well, apparently no one."

podcast.body: This album features the song "Behind the Wheel," which has spawned an unquantifiable number of remixes. "There have been so many remixes of behind the wheel from music for the masses, both of the legal and illegal variety that no one, no one in the Peshmo knows exactly how many there are."
